title: What teachers should learn: An alternative graduate school curriculum e-school-curriculum
author: Daniel Buck
source: The Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 24, 2026
summary: Following his report criticizing coursework at ten graduate schools of education, Daniel Buck takes up the harder task of proposing what teachers should study instead. He would ideally reduce education to a licensing certificate attached to a content major, but here sketches a 10 to 12 course master's program for classroom teachers. The syllabus balances philosophy, methods, policy, history, special education, and content knowledge, running from Richard Gamble's The Great Tradition through Freire, Dewey, and Hirsch to practical titles by Marzano, Sherrington, Bennett, Willingham, and Kirschner and Hendrick. Buck stresses that only one program he reviewed offered a course on cognitive science despite its relevance to working memory and cognitive load, and he insists policy courses set opposing ideas side by side. Four courses in the teacher's content area reflect research that subject knowledge improves teaching. He concludes that teachers deserve a command of their subject and profession rather than ideological hectoring.
points: Buck would ideally make education a minor or licensing certificate attached to a content major, with two methods courses and student teaching.
His philosophy sequence pairs the classical tradition via Gamble's The Great Tradition with Freire, Dewey, and Hirsch so teachers know the landmark theorists.
Only one of the ten programs he reviewed included a course dedicated to cognitive science.
Policy courses should set opposing views side by side rather than peddle one approved narrative.
Four content-area courses reflect research that a teacher's subject knowledge improves their teaching.
quotes: Now I like to believe that these “spot the woke” exercises are useful insofar as they expose malpractice and ideological drift. They’re most certainly fun. But I also acknowledge the old truism that criticism is easier than proffering solutions or alternatives.

Were I made Supreme Chancellor over American education, I’d delegate “education” as a minor or licensing certificate attached to a content major—two methods courses and a student teaching assignment tacked onto another major with reduced course loads elsewhere.

Only one program that I reviewed included any course dedicated specifically to cognitive science, even though its findings on automaticity, working memory, cognitive load, and chunking are incredibly pertinent to the classroom.
There are many quality options for surveys and overviews of education policy. What matters is setting opposing ideas alongside each other instead of peddling one “approved” narrative.
Through philosophy, teachers understand the ends of education, recognize the assumptions behind competing approaches, and can thus make wiser instructional choices.

A teacher should emerge from graduate school with a deeper command of his subject, a broader understanding of his profession, and a better idea of what to do when 25 students walk through the door on Monday morning.
